shown as the progress figure on a port's fleet-hunting job
shown as the progress figure on a sovereign's fleet-hunting quest

globalVars.name: gameOvers
globalVars.description: A lifetime tally of how many times the run has ended in defeat and dropped the player back to the main menu. Places that forbid a game over - the arena, and the generated ruins, where losing has its own consequence - do not count. Nothing in the game consults it, so it is a running record for a mod or a curious player.

setBy.note: raised by one as the defeat sequence begins, before the game fades back to the main menu

globalVars.notes: An area that forbids defeat runs its own scripted response instead and returns before the tally is touched, so losing in such a place never counts. Nothing resets it.

globalVars.name: gateGravenOpen
globalVars.description: Marks that the graven gate on the opening shore has been made to work. It is raised at the moment the gate carries the party through for the first time. Afterwards the world map dresses that spot as an open gateway on arrival and lets the player step through it whenever they like, and the companion who was pressing the player to investigate the gate stops raising the subject.

setBy.note: raised as the gate carries the party out to the world map for the first time

readBy.note: one trigger stages the gate opening the first time the player arrives at that spot on the map; another lets stepping onto the gate carry them through to the cove thereafter
the companion's prompting about the gate is withdrawn once it is positive

globalVars.name: gen{index}

params.name: index
params.note: one to five; only those five names are ever named

globalVars.description: Five markers meant to hold whatever a settlement most recently generated - its wares, its faces, or some other rotating detail. The only thing that touches them is a bulk reset that would blank all five when a settlement's services are refreshed; nothing reads them, and that reset is never fired by the game's own content.

setBy.note: all five are zeroed together as part of the settlement-refresh reset; that trigger is never fired by the game itself, so in practice this never happens

globalVars.name: goal{index}

params.name: index
params.note: zero to fifty-three; the slots are filled from the lowest free one upwards, eighteen to a journal page

setBy.note: writes the goal's text into the lowest empty slot, and refuses if a slot already holds the same text
rewrites every slot when the list is compacted, closing up gaps left by removed goals
removes the slots past the end of the compacted list outright

searched for the goal being dropped, so the list can be closed up around it
the highest filled slot decides how many pages of goals the journal shows
answers whether a goal with given text is on the list at all
counts the goals outstanding, and its companion counts those finished

globalVars.name: goal{index}Done

params.name: index
params.note: zero to fifty-three, matching the goal slot it belongs to

globalVars.description: Whether the goal in the matching slot has been struck through as finished. It holds nothing while the goal is outstanding and the word that means struck-through once it is done - which is also how the journal knows to draw a line across it. Adding a goal to a slot clears it, so a reused slot never starts out already ticked.

setBy.note: marked struck-through when a goal is ticked off, which also flashes the journal line and awards the crew a little experience
removed as a goal is written into the slot, so a reused slot starts out unfinished
carried along with its goal when the list is compacted
removed for slots whose goal is outstanding, and for slots past the end of the compacted list

readBy.note: only an outstanding goal can be ticked off, and a goal already struck through is left alone
answers whether a goal with given text has been finished
separates outstanding goals from finished ones when counting

The only value the game ever writes is the one that means struck-through; any other non-zero text would also read as finished to the counting operators but would be treated as unfinished by the tick-off itself.

globalVars.name: gotZapRod
globalVars.description: Marks that the player has taken the lightning wand from its stand in the sunken tower. A check by the doorway watches the stand: once the wand is gone and this has not yet been raised, a chime of approval plays and the flag goes up, so the moment is acknowledged exactly once however many times the player walks past.

setBy.note: raised the first time the player crosses the doorway with the wand no longer on its stand

readBy.note: the same trigger abandons itself when the flag is already up, so the chime plays only once

globalVars.notes: It belongs to one hand-authored tower and has no meaning elsewhere. Nothing clears it, and nothing else reads it - taking the wand back to the stand would not lower it.

globalVars.name: gpCollect_{locationID}

params.name: locationID
params.note: a port the player has founded and owns; the name is composed from whichever port the player is standing in

globalVars.description: The takings a player-owned port has piled up waiting to be collected. Walking into the port tots up everything earned since the figure was last touched - a rate set by how many businesses the port has and how experienced their keepers are - and adds it on. Asking the port's manager for the money hands over the whole sum and drops it back to nothing.

setBy.note: on arrival at the port, rewritten as its previous contents plus the earnings accrued since it was last written
seeded at one when the player founds the port
dropped to nothing as the manager hands the money over

readBy.note: how long ago it was last written is the period the new earnings are calculated over, and is also what the port's keepers gain experience for
the manager quotes the standing figure, and it is the sum actually paid out

globalVars.notes: Because the accrual is driven by how long ago the figure was last written, the manager's own payout resets that clock too, and so does every arrival at the port. A companion variable records when the money was last actually collected, which is what the manager quotes as 'over the past so many days'.

globalVars.name: grovesDiscovered
globalVars.description: How many groves the player has charted. It rises by one each time a previously unknown place tagged as a grove is spotted from the world map. Reaching fifteen earns the matching achievement. If the world's generated places ever have to be laid out again, the count is zeroed along with them so it stays in step with what is actually out there.

setBy.note: raised by one when a newly spotted place carries the grove tag, at the same moment the player is credited with exploration renown for the find
zeroed when the world's generated places are torn down and laid out afresh

readBy.note: fifteen or more earns the grove-finding achievement

globalVars.notes: The reset only runs when the world's generated places are rebuilt, which the game itself only does after a failed layout attempt; in ordinary play the count only grows.

globalVars.name: growthport22
globalVars.description: Counts how many times the player has cast growth magic on a particular scholar's garden. Any positive count unlocks a one-off remark from the scholar, who notices what was done to his plants and holds forth on why growth magic makes for bitter fruit. He only says it once; after that his ordinary line comes back.

setBy.note: raised by one whenever growth magic lands on the garden patch, with no limit on repeats

readBy.note: any positive count offers the scholar's remark, and having heard it once cancels it out for good

globalVars.notes: It belongs to one hand-authored garden and has no meaning elsewhere. It counts rather than latches, but the only reader treats anything above zero the same.

globalVars.name: hideTravelUI
globalVars.description: Clears the interface off the screen. While it is positive the travel bar is hidden outright and the surrounding panels - character stats, quick slots, the party strip - stop being refreshed and stay as they are. Scripted sequences raise it so the screen is uncluttered for a scene, and lower it when the player has control back.

setBy.note: raised for a scripted sequence, alongside suppressing the post-battle autosave
lowered once the opening beach sequence hands control back
lowered immediately by the shortcut that skips the opening sequence

readBy.note: the travel bar is hidden and its refresh abandoned for the frame
the surrounding panels are left untouched, so whatever state they were in persists

globalVars.notes: It stops the panels being updated rather than hiding them, so anything already on screen when it goes up stays on screen. Both readers run every frame, so raising and lowering it takes effect immediately.

globalVars.name: hireCrewGoalDone
globalVars.description: Marks that the player has been shown the little ceremony for reaching a crew of five: the journal opens, the goal is written in and immediately struck through. It is raised as part of that ceremony so it plays only once, however many times the crew is taken up to five afterwards.

setBy.note: raised a second and a half into the ceremony, between the journal opening and the goal being struck through

readBy.note: its own requirement: the ceremony only runs while the crew has reached five and this has not yet been raised

globalVars.notes: The goal is added and completed in one go rather than being something the player works towards, so this flag is what makes the whole sequence one-off. Nothing lowers it.

globalVars.name: ignis_enc1
globalVars.description: Meant to record that the player has met the fire creature the first time, in a jungle. It serves two chambers at once: while it stands at nothing the jungle keeps offering that first meeting, and the reef's follow-up meeting is always passed over. Raising it would swap the two round. Nothing in the game ever raises it, so the first meeting stays available forever and the follow-up never appears.

readBy.note: used directly as the chance of rejecting the first fire-creature chamber when picking the room at the heart of a generated jungle
one minus this value, plus the follow-up marker, is the chance of rejecting the reef's fire-creature chamber - so at nothing the reef chamber is always rejected

globalVars.notes: There is no writer anywhere - not in the game's code and not in its content - so the reef's fire-creature chamber can never be laid out. A mod that wants the pair to work has to raise this after the first meeting.

globalVars.name: ignis_enc_2nd1
globalVars.description: Meant to record that the player has already had the follow-up meeting with the fire creature out on a reef, so that chamber is passed over when a reef is laid out again. Nothing in the game ever raises it, and the chamber it guards is unreachable for a separate reason, so it has no effect as shipped.

readBy.note: added into the rejection chance for the reef's fire-creature chamber, so any positive value keeps that chamber out

globalVars.notes: There is no writer anywhere - not in the game's code and not in its content. The chamber it guards is in any case never laid out, because the first-meeting marker it is paired with is never raised either.

globalVars.name: ignoreHardcore
globalVars.description: Lifts the restriction that saving is only allowed in port. While it is at one or more, the game may save wherever the player happens to be, whatever the difficulty setting says. A new game raises it so the opening can save freely, and the opening beach lowers it once the player is out in the world proper.

setBy.note: raised as a new game begins, so the opening is not hemmed in by the save restriction
lowered once the opening beach sequence is behind the player
lowered immediately by the shortcut that skips the opening sequence

readBy.note: one or more permits saving outright, checked after the difficulty option that allows it everywhere and before the tests for being in or heading to a port

globalVars.notes: It only matters when the difficulty setting restricts saving to ports; with that restriction off, saving is allowed anyway. Certain scripted saves bypass the whole question and are unaffected.

globalVars.name: incOnNewDay_{dialogNodeID}

params.name: dialogNodeID
params.note: the speaker's current default conversation node, not the node the effect is written in

globalVars.description: How many times a townsperson has given one particular greeting, and when they last gave it. It lets a shopkeeper work steadily through a series of greetings rather than repeating the first one: the next time the player talks to them, if a full day has passed since that greeting was last used, they move on to the following one in the series. The count itself rises on every telling; only the time of the last telling decides whether they advance.

setBy.note: raised by one every time the speaker gives the greeting, which also refreshes the moment it was last given

readBy.note: the speaker moves on to the next greeting in the series only when the count is already positive and a full day has passed since it was last written

globalVars.notes: The name is taken from the speaker's default conversation node at the moment of speaking, so as they advance through the series each greeting gets its own separate record. The very first telling only starts the clock; the speaker cannot advance until they have given a greeting at least once.

globalVars.name: innkeeper_chat
globalVars.description: A marker meant to say the innkeeper has a fresh remark ready for the player. The only thing that touches it is a bulk reset that raises it back to 1 when a settlement's services are refreshed; nothing reads it, and that reset is never fired by the game's own content.

setBy.note: raised to 1 as part of the settlement-refresh reset; that trigger is never fired by the game itself, so in practice this never happens

globalVars.notes: Effectively dead alongside the other four townsfolk remark markers: no reader consults it, and the trigger that names it is unreachable. A mod is free to claim the name.

globalVars.name: investigatorAnswer_{actorID}

params.name: actorID
params.note: the investigator the player commissioned, taken from whoever they are talking to when the answer is prepared

globalVars.description: The written-out result of an investigation the player commissioned, in the words the investigator will use to deliver it. It is composed when the job is worked out - the bearing of the nearest uncharted place, where the next big demand for goods will be, what creature was researched, whose fleet movements were traced - and is then read out when the player comes back for it, and again whenever they ask to hear it repeated. Each investigator keeps their own.

setBy.note: written with the name and bearing of the nearest place the player has not charted, or an apology if they have charted them all
written with the port and goods of the next great demand
written with the creature that was researched, or an apology if the player's journal already covers everything they have killed
written with the faction whose fleet movements were traced, or an apology if the faction was not recognised

readBy.note: printed word for word as the investigator's report, and again on the repeat-the-report branch
the option to hear the report again is only offered when this holds text rather than a number

globalVars.notes: The name is composed from whoever the player is talking to at the moment the answer is prepared, so commissioning a second investigator does not overwrite the first one's report. Nothing clears it, so the last report stands until that investigator is given another job.

globalVars.name: investigatorTask_{actorID}

params.name: actorID
params.note: the investigator the player commissioned, taken from whoever they are talking to when the job is worked out

globalVars.description: A piece of work the investigator will carry out on the player's behalf when they hand in their report - written out as an instruction rather than as a value. Two of the investigations use it: one adds the researched creature to the player's journal, the other switches on thirty days of tracking for a faction's fleets. setBy.note: written with an instruction to add the researched creature to the journal, only when there is something the player has killed but not yet researched
written with an instruction to switch on thirty-day tracking for the named faction's fleets
emptied immediately after being carried out, so the work is not repeated

readBy.note: carried out as the report is delivered, and skipped entirely when the value is empty

globalVars.name: laganDefeated
globalVars.description: Marks that the rival commodore who has been hunting the player has finally been beaten at sea. It is raised during his defeat scene. Afterwards the travelling companion stops offering to discuss what to do about his fleet, and the wider conversation about the party's long-term aims closes once both of its open questions have been settled.

setBy.note: raised in the commodore's own defeat scene, which is picked out by matching him against the last commodore beaten

readBy.note: the 'about the fleet' reply is withdrawn once it is positive, and it is one of the two questions that between them close off the long-term-goals conversation

globalVars.notes: Nothing clears it. It is raised by the defeat scene rather than by the battle itself, so a player who somehow skips that scene would not have it raised.

globalVars.name: laganFleetSpawned
globalVars.description: Marks that the rival commodore's fleet has been put on the map outside the storm cove. It is raised as that fleet appears, three days into the story, along with the obstacles that pen the player in until the fleet is dealt with. With it raised, the cove opens a way back inland; while it is still down, straying too far from the cove instead prompts a nudge that the player is going the wrong way.

setBy.note: raised as the rival fleet is placed outside the cove, three days in, alongside the barriers that hem the water in

readBy.note: once the fleet is gone but the flag stands, the barriers are cleared and the matching journal goal is struck off; while the flag is down, wandering away prompts a wrong-way conversation
the passage back inland from the cove only works once the fleet has appeared

globalVars.notes: It says the fleet was placed, not that it survives; the barrier-clearing trigger pairs it with a separate check that no such fleet is on the map any more. Nothing clears it.

globalVars.name: lastCommodoreDefeated
globalVars.description: Who commanded the last enemy fleet the player sank. It is emptied at the start of every won sea battle and then filled in, if that fleet had a named commander, once the sinking is confirmed. It picks out which commander's defeat scene plays, and it keeps that commander from being handed a fresh fleet straight away.

setBy.note: emptied at the top of every won sea battle, before the fleet is accounted for
filled in with the beaten fleet's commander once the sinking goes through

readBy.note: each commander's defeat scene is chosen by matching this against them
a commander named here is struck off the list of candidates when a faction is looking for someone to lead a new fleet

globalVars.notes: It holds nothing when the beaten fleet had no named commander, and stays empty until the next such victory. Because only the most recent name is kept, a commander only stays off the candidate list until someone else is beaten.

globalVars.name: lastExecutedActionActorID
globalVars.description: Who used the ability most recently put into play. It is written at the same moment as the ability itself, and is left empty when the ability came from the world rather than from a character - a trap going off, or an effect cast from a tile. Nothing in the game consults it; it is kept so a mod's own conditions can ask who just acted.

setBy.note: written with the character beginning the ability, or emptied when the ability has no caster
written again when the ability actually goes off, or emptied when it has no caster

globalVars.notes: Abilities marked as not delaying others are skipped, so quick incidental effects do not disturb the record. It is only ever overwritten, never removed, so between battles it still names whoever acted last.

globalVars.name: lastExecutedActionID
globalVars.description: The ability most recently put into play, whether by a character or by the world itself. It is written both when an ability begins and when it actually goes off. Abilities that are marked as not holding up anything else - small incidental effects - are skipped, so the record follows the meaningful actions. Nothing in the game consults it; it is kept so a mod's own conditions can ask what just happened.

setBy.note: written as an ability begins, in both the character-cast and world-cast forms
written again as the ability actually goes off

globalVars.notes: It is only ever overwritten, never removed, so between battles it still names the last ability used. The assignments deliberately skip the achievement sweep that ordinarily follows a global-variable write, because they happen constantly.

globalVars.name: lastExecutedAvAffecterActorID
globalVars.description: Who was responsible for the most recent stat-changing effect to land. It is written alongside the effect itself, and left empty when the effect came from the world rather than from a character - a lingering patch of fire, say. Only effects that are marked as worth recording update it. Nothing in the game consults it; it is kept so a mod's own conditions can ask who is behind what just happened.

setBy.note: written with the character behind the effect, or emptied when there is none, and only for effects flagged as worth recording
the same, for an effect that lingers on a tile and goes off later

globalVars.notes: An effect not flagged as worth recording leaves the previous name standing, so the record can name someone other than the source of the effect that just landed. It is only ever overwritten, never removed.

globalVars.name: lastExecutedAvAffecterID
globalVars.description: The most recent stat-changing effect to land on someone - the individual piece of an ability that heals, wounds or applies a condition, rather than the ability as a whole. Only effects marked as worth recording update it. Nothing in the game consults it; it is kept so a mod's own conditions can ask what just landed.

setBy.note: written as the effect lands on its target, after its own conditions have been met, and only for effects flagged as worth recording
the same, for an effect that lingers on a tile and goes off later; here the name written is the ability the lingering effect came from

globalVars.notes: The two writers do not agree on what they store: one writes the effect's own identifier, the other writes the identifier of the ability that left the lingering patch. It is only ever overwritten, never removed.

globalVars.name: lastFoodEaten
globalVars.description: The dish the crew most recently sat down to at a tavern. Both what it holds and when it was written matter: the tavern will not sell the crew another meal until twenty hours have passed, offering a greyed-out 'already ate today' instead, and the dish named here is what gets put on the table as a prop for the meal scene and taken away again afterwards.

setBy.note: written with the dish just bought, after its effects have been applied to everyone aboard

readBy.note: the offer to buy a meal is only live once twenty hours have passed since the last one, or if the crew have never eaten
puts the named dish on the table as a prop for the meal scene
takes that prop away again

globalVars.notes: The twenty-hour wait is measured from when the value was last written, so a mod that rewrites it - even with the same dish - lets the crew eat again straight away. Nothing clears it.

globalVars.name: lastProcZoneEntry
globalVars.description: The way in to the most recently generated set of caverns or ruins. It is written as the first room of a generated place is laid out, so the game can find its way back to that entrance later. Content uses it as the destination for a move that means 'go to the entrance of the place we just made', including the retreat out of a fight in such a place.

setBy.note: written with the name of the room being laid out, but only for the room marked as the entrance

readBy.note: the destination for a move to the generated entrance; in combat it becomes the place the party would retreat to
the same move reached as a trigger effect rather than a task

globalVars.notes: It is overwritten every time a new generated place is laid out, and never cleared, so it always names the most recent one.

globalVars.name: lastReactionActionActorID
globalVars.description: Who last hit back. When a character has a standing reaction - a riposte, a counter, an ability that fires when something happens to them - and it goes off, this records the character doing the reacting. Nothing in the game consults it; it is kept so a mod's own conditions can ask who just retaliated.

setBy.note: written as the reaction fires, once every check on whether the character may react has passed

globalVars.notes: Reactions marked as not holding up other actions are skipped, so the record follows the meaningful ones. It is only ever overwritten, never removed.

globalVars.name: lastReactionActionCasterID
globalVars.description: Who provoked the last reaction - the character whose blow or effect the reacting character was answering. It is only written when there was somebody to blame; a reaction to something impersonal, such as walking into fire, leaves the previous name standing. Nothing in the game consults it; it is kept so a mod's own conditions can ask who set a retaliation off.

setBy.note: written with the character who caused the reaction, and skipped entirely when the cause was impersonal

globalVars.notes: Because it is skipped rather than emptied when there is no culprit, it can name someone from an earlier exchange while the companion records describe the current one. It is only ever overwritten, never removed.

globalVars.name: lastReactionActionID
globalVars.description: The ability that last went off as a reaction rather than as a deliberate act - a riposte, a counter, or anything a character throws back when something happens to them. Nothing in the game consults it; it is kept so a mod's own conditions can ask what was just triggered in retaliation.

setBy.note: written as the reaction fires, once every check on whether the character may react has passed

globalVars.notes: Reactions marked as not holding up other actions are skipped, so the record follows the meaningful ones. It is written before the ability is actually cast, and only ever overwritten, never removed.

globalVars.name: lastVisit
globalVars.description: How many hours had passed since the player was last in the area they have just walked into. It is worked out on arrival, from the moment they last left that same area, and it is what the area itself uses to catch up on the time it missed - rolling its clock forward day by day. Arriving somewhere for the first time, or leaving an area, leaves it at nothing.

setBy.note: written on arrival with the hours elapsed since the player last left this same area
zeroed on the way out of an area, so an unfamiliar arrival reads as no time gone by

globalVars.notes: It is measured in hours of world time and is rewritten on every arrival, so it describes the area the player is standing in now. Nothing in the game reads it back - the day-catching-up it accompanies uses the same figure directly - so it is there for a mod's own conditions.

globalVars.name: lastVisit_days
globalVars.description: How many whole days had passed since the player was last in the area they have just walked into. It governs whether a settlement has moved on in their absence: at more than a day, the tavern puts a fresh set of faces up for hire, and the previous batch of casual hangers-on is cleared away.

setBy.note: written on arrival with the whole days elapsed since the player last left this same area

readBy.note: more than a day away is one of the conditions for the tavern to put fresh faces up for hire
more than a day away clears out the hangers-on left over from the previous visit

globalVars.notes: Unlike the hour-by-hour figure it sits beside, this one is not zeroed when the player leaves an area, so on a first arrival somewhere it still holds whatever the previous arrival left. Nothing clears it.

globalVars.name: learnedPassive
globalVars.description: Counts how many passive abilities the player has unlocked. Its real job is to catch the very first one: because nothing under that name exists yet at that moment, the game knows to put up a reminder that a passive still has to be equipped before it does anything. Every unlock after that simply adds to the count and the reminder is not shown again.

setBy.note: seeded at one the first time a passive is unlocked, which is also when the equip-it reminder is put on screen for thirteen seconds
raised by one on every later unlock

readBy.note: the reminder is shown only when nothing has ever been stored under the name, which distinguishes 'never unlocked one' from a count of zero

globalVars.notes: The test is for the name existing at all rather than for its value, so a mod that writes zero there suppresses the reminder just as effectively as one that writes a large number. Nothing clears it.

globalVars.name: magi_chat
globalVars.description: A marker meant to say the magic-goods seller has a fresh remark ready for the player. The only thing that touches it is a bulk reset that raises it back to 1 when a settlement's services are refreshed; nothing reads it, and that reset is never fired by the game's own content.

setBy.note: raised to 1 as part of the settlement-refresh reset; that trigger is never fired by the game itself, so in practice this never happens

globalVars.notes: Effectively dead alongside the other four townsfolk remark markers: no reader consults it, and the trigger that names it is unreachable. A mod is free to claim the name.

globalVars.name: mapCompleted
globalVars.description: Marks that the player has charted the whole world and reported it to their cartographer. It is raised during that final report, which also pays a large bonus, awards a great deal of exploration renown, and lifts the fog from the entire map for good. Cartographers greet a player carrying it as the famous explorer they have become.

setBy.note: raised when a report puts the charted share at a hundred percent, alongside clearing the map's fog outright

readBy.note: any positive value awards the full-map achievement
replaces the cartographer's greeting with one that recognises the player as a famous explorer

globalVars.notes: The charted share is scaled so that ninety-four percent of the map's area counts as a hundred percent, since the rest is open sea that cannot be charted. Nothing clears it.

globalVars.name: mapPercentPaid
globalVars.description: The share of the world the player has already been paid for charting, as a fraction between nothing and one. Each report to a cartographer pays only for the ground covered since the last one, so the difference between this and the share charted now is what earns money; the figure is then brought up to date. globalVars.name: tradeGoodPriceDistanceMod
globalVars.description: Adjusts how much a trade good gains in price simply for having been carried a long way from where it is produced. It is added to the flat bonus the game already pays per unit of distance to the nearest place that makes that good, so raising it makes long hauls pay better across the board and lowering it flattens the trade map out. It has no built-in setter and exists for mods to tune.

The adjusted price is what the player sees quoted, and the difference it makes is broken out to the player as the distance bonus on the good's description. Setting it far enough negative makes distant goods worthless rather than valuable, since nothing floors the result before the price is rounded down.

globalVars.name: tradeGoodPriceDistanceMultMod

It has no built-in setter and exists for mods to tune.

setBy.note: the game never writes it; left unset it counts as nothing and the built-in rate stands

Because the three adjustments compound, changing this one shifts what the other two are working from. Nothing keeps the rate above minus one, so a mod that pushes it far negative turns long hauls into debts.

globalVars.name: tradeGoodPriceDistanceSquaredMultMod

It is added to a very small built-in rate that is charged against the square of the distance from the nearest place producing the good, which is what makes a haul across the world worth disproportionately more than two hauls of half the length. It has no built-in setter and exists for mods to tune.

globalVars.notes: Because the distance is squared before the rate is applied, a change here bites far harder at long range than the plain proportional rate does, and the built-in value is correspondingly tiny - a mod adding even a hundredth to it makes distant goods absurdly valuable. The distance used is the shortest run from where the player is standing to any place in the same part of the world that produces the good; a good with no producer nearby gets no distance adjustment at all.

globalVars.name: tradeProfitTotal
globalVars.description: A lifetime tally of the money the player has made purely from trading well - the part of each sale that came from selling a good far from where it is produced or into a hungry market, over and above what the goods would have fetched on their plain worth. A sale that fetches no more than the plain worth adds nothing. Nothing in the game reads the tally back.

setBy.note: the surplus over the plain worth is added as each sale is completed, and the same surplus is what earns the player trade renown

globalVars.notes: Only sales made through a shop counter are counted, and only the surplus, so it is a much smaller figure than total money earned. Nothing resets it.

globalVars.name: tradeSpecial_goodsID
globalVars.description: The commodity one port is paying double for this month. Its trader greets the player by asking after it and promising twice the going rate the first time a load is sold there, and rumours in other towns name it as the month's big demand. It is drawn fresh each month together with the port, and it is emptied the moment the player takes the trader up on the offer.

setBy.note: a new game starts with grain as the standing demand
at each month's turn the commodity announced a month earlier becomes the current one
emptied as soon as a load is sold at the port that wanted it, so the doubled rate is paid once and not again
put back unchanged after an investigator forces a draw on a game that had none, so paying for the tip does not move the current demand

selling it there does not depress that port's prices the way an ordinary sale would
the doubling is called out on the goods' description while the player is standing in that port
townsfolk elsewhere name it as the commodity in demand this month
the trader at that port opens by asking after it by name and offering double for the first load

The pair is drawn without reference to what the player is carrying or can reach.

globalVars.description: The port paying double for one commodity this month. Its trader offers twice the going rate for the first load brought in, and townsfolk in other ports pass on word of where the demand is. It is drawn fresh at each month's turn along with the commodity, and it is emptied as soon as the player collects on the offer.

setBy.note: a new game starts with the demand sitting at one fixed port
at each month's turn the port announced a month earlier becomes the current one
emptied as soon as the wanted load is sold there, so the doubled rate is paid once and not again
put back unchanged after an investigator forces a draw on a game that had none, so paying for the tip does not move the current demand

the sale here does not depress this port's prices the way an ordinary sale would
the doubling is called out on the goods' description while the player is standing here
townsfolk elsewhere name this port as where the demand is, unless the month is nearly out

Rumours stop naming it in the last third of each month, so a player who hears one still has time to sail there. Emptying leaves it as blank text rather than removing it, and no port has a blank identifier, so an emptied demand matches nowhere.

globalVars.name: trainer_chat
globalVars.description: A marker meant to say the skills trainer has a fresh remark ready for the player. The only thing that touches it is a bulk reset that raises it back to 1 when a settlement's services are refreshed; nothing reads it, and that reset is never fired by the game's own content.

setBy.note: raised to 1 as part of the settlement-refresh reset; that trigger is never fired by the game itself, so in practice this never happens

globalVars.notes: Effectively dead alongside the other four townsfolk remark markers: no reader consults it, and the trigger that names it is unreachable. A mod is free to claim the name.

globalVars.name: treasureTCX
globalVars.description: The east-west position on the world map of a wreck the player has been sent to salvage. It is written down when a guild hands over the job, at the same moment the hand-drawn map with its cross is made from the surrounding sea. The next time the player puts to sea, a buried wreck stuffed with coin, lost cargo and papers is planted at that spot for the player to find with a look around, and the note is torn up so it cannot be planted twice.

setBy.note: recorded from the spot the salvage job points at, the same spot the drawn map is centred on
zeroed as the wreck is planted, so putting to sea again does not plant another

readBy.note: the spot the wreck is buried at; a zero here means no job is outstanding and nothing is planted
the planting is attempted a moment after the player puts to sea

globalVars.notes: Only the east-west figure is checked for being set, so the pair counts as outstanding whenever it is not zero. A wreck genuinely at the far western edge of the map, at column zero, would therefore never be planted - the game's own salvage jobs never point there. The wreck is planted buried, so it has to be dug up rather than simply walked onto.

globalVars.name: treasureTCY
globalVars.description: The north-south position on the world map of a wreck the player has been sent to salvage. It is written down when a guild hands over the job, alongside the east-west figure and the hand-drawn map that marks the spot with a cross. When the player next puts to sea, a buried wreck full of coin, lost cargo and papers is planted there, and the note is torn up.

setBy.note: recorded from the spot the salvage job points at, the same spot the drawn map is centred on
zeroed as the wreck is planted, so putting to sea again does not plant another

readBy.note: supplies the north-south half of the spot the wreck is buried at
the planting is attempted a moment after the player puts to sea

globalVars.notes: Unlike its east-west companion this one is never tested for being set: whether a wreck is outstanding is decided by the other figure alone. A mod that writes only this one leaves the pair looking unset, and one that zeroes only the other leaves this one holding a stale figure that is never looked at again.

globalVars.name: turnNumber
globalVars.description: A running count of turns that have gone by, ticking up every time the order of play moves on - whenever a character's turn begins, a timed effect comes due or a queued action goes off, whether the party is fighting or simply walking about. It is what lets the game tell apart blows that land within the same turn, which is how a character's resistance to being hit repeatedly is worked out.

setBy.note: one per step of the order of play, counted after whatever that step was has happened

readBy.note: stamped onto a character as the turn they last lost health on

a further wound on the same stamped turn, while the running damage figure is still showing, is softened in proportion to the target's resistance to repeated hits and to the damage already taken that turn

globalVars.notes: It counts every step of the order of play, not rounds of a fight, so it climbs while the party is merely travelling and it is never reset - it keeps rising for the life of the save. Do not treat it as a fight's turn count; it is only ever compared for equality with itself, so its absolute size never matters to the game.

globalVars.name: turnsTaken
globalVars.description: A lifetime count of turns the party has taken in battle, ticking up each time the order of play comes round to a new turn in a fight. Its main job is spotting a player's very first fight: the on-screen prompts explaining how to move, aim and attack are shown only while the count is still at one or below and the player is on mouse and keyboard. It is also shown to the player as the turns-taken line on the personal statistics screen and again in the closing credits.

setBy.note: one per turn as the order of play comes round in a fight
the developers' shortcut past the opening sets it straight to one, so a skipped start does not leave the beginner prompts on
the same, for the option that skips the opening scene

readBy.note: the very first turn of all - the count not merely being low but never having been written - is what puts up the prompt telling the player how to move
after a first move, the prompt explaining how to attack
while moving, the prompt to click a tile
after a first attack, the prompt for what to do next
clears the standing prompt when a chosen action is called off
printed as the turns-taken line on the personal statistics screen
printed again as the turns-taken line in the closing credits

globalVars.notes: Nothing resets it, so after the first fight the beginner prompts never come back. The prompts are also withheld from anyone playing on a controller, which has its own on-screen guidance. Because the very first prompt keys off the count never having been written rather than its value, a mod that writes a zero into it before the first fight suppresses that one prompt while leaving the rest.

globalVars.name: valueThisRun
globalVars.description: What the last expedition was worth when the party came home: the coin they were carrying, plus what the loot they brought back fetches, plus a fixed sum for each unlock recovered and a small bonus for the experience the survivors earned. It is worked out on the results screen and decides how the crew react - flatly for a trip that made nothing, warmly for one that made a fortune - with a separate line depending on how many of the party died.

setBy.note: worked out as the results screen is built and overwritten each time, so it always describes the most recent trip
the same reckoning, reached as a trigger effect rather than a task

readBy.note: sorts the trip into four bands - nothing, little, fair or a fortune - and picks the crew's remark from the ones written for that band and for the number of deaths, preferring lines the player has heard least often
meant to decide whether the crew left behind recover fully while the party is out; the test is written so that they always do
the same, reached as a trigger effect

globalVars.notes: It describes one trip only and is replaced wholesale at the end of the next, so it is never a running total despite reading like money. The bands are fixed at the coin figures twenty, sixty and three hundred, so a mod that changes what loot is worth changes which remark the crew make. The barracks check that would consult it is short-circuited and never actually looks at the value.

globalVars.name: vineWither
globalVars.description: Thins the vine-folk out of the jungle. The knots of vine creatures that the game considers planting at the heart of each room while it lays out a jungle are normally always taken; raising this makes each one likely to be passed over instead, leaving the room to something else. Nothing in the game ever raises it, so the jungle grows its full complement unless a mod says otherwise.

setBy.note: no site in the game or its content writes it; left alone it counts as nothing

readBy.note: each of the five vine-creature centrepieces is rejected with a chance of three tenths of this value as the jungle is laid out

globalVars.notes: Each whole unit adds roughly a one-in-three chance of a vine knot being skipped, so a value of one leaves two thirds of them standing and a value of three or more clears them out entirely. Nothing keeps it in range: a negative value makes the knots certain rather than merely likely, which is what they already are. It applies to jungle layouts only, and to those five pieces within them; vine creatures placed by hand elsewhere are untouched.

globalVars.name: worldTimeOnFootMult
globalVars.description: How fast the clock and the calendar run while the player is walking about on foot. The game does not normally let time pass at all on land - hours only go by at sea - and this is the knob that changes that: set to one, an hour of walking costs as much of the day as an hour of sailing, and the party eats through their stores at the same rate. It makes no difference at sea, where time always passes at its ordinary rate.

setBy.note: no site in the game or its content writes it; left alone it counts as nothing, which is why land travel costs no time

readBy.note: scales the time charged for each moment the party spends walking, and is overridden to the ordinary rate whenever the thing the player is steering is a ship

globalVars.notes: Time only accrues while the party is actually moving and free to act, so standing still, talking or being held in a scene costs nothing regardless. Charging time on foot also spends provisions and wears on the crew's spirits, the same as time at sea, so raising this makes long overland journeys a real drain rather than free. A negative value turns the clock backwards while walking, which nothing guards against.

globalVars.name: zoneGenFailed
globalVars.description: Marks that laying out one of the world's generated places went wrong and left a stub of a map instead of a real one. It is raised as the bad layout is written out, and while it stands the world-building sequence throws the whole generated world away and builds it again from scratch, lowering the mark as it does so.

setBy.note: raised when the finished layout comes out a single tile across, which means the attempt collapsed
lowered as the world is thrown away and rebuilt, so a second failure is needed to set the retry going again

readBy.note: a moment after the world's places have been settled, the rebuild is set going only if the mark is standing
the rebuild also checks the mark itself, so firing it by hand on a sound world does nothing

globalVars.notes: It says only that something went wrong, not which place; the response is to rebuild everything rather than retry the one layout. Because the rebuild lowers it before generating afresh, a run of failures retries once per pass of the world-building sequence rather than looping on the spot. The bad layout is still written out to the save before the mark is raised.

globalVars.name: zone_travel4_enabled
globalVars.description: Keeps the spider nest out of the heart of the deepest jungle. The rooms of that layout are given their centrepiece from a fixed list tried in order, and the nest is first in line; raising this makes it certain to be passed over, so those rooms get whatever comes next instead. Nothing in the game ever raises it.

setBy.note: no site in the game or its content writes it; left alone it counts as nothing and the nest is placed as usual

readBy.note: added into the chance of passing over the spider nest, alongside a term that already accounts for how large a party the player may bring

globalVars.notes: It shares its reader with the party-size knob, so the two add together: raising this by one is enough on its own to guarantee the skip whatever the other says. A fraction partly applies rather than doing nothing, and a negative value pushes the other way, making the nest more certain than it already is. It affects the deepest jungle layout only. Its name suggests it was meant to go with a fourth way in or out of that place, but nothing else in the game refers to any such thing.

globalVars.name: {actorClassID}_XP

params.name: actorClassID
params.note: the trade the experience was earned in; a character fighting under a borrowed trade credits the borrowed one

globalVars.description: How much experience the player's people have earned in one trade over the whole game, counted as a house record rather than against any one person. Only experience someone earns in their own right is counted, so passing knowledge on does not inflate it. It is the yardstick newcomers are measured against: anyone joining or coming back from the reserve is brought up to a small fraction of it, and while the crew are sharing what they know, everyone is handed a slice of it as well.

setBy.note: added to by every award a character earns in their own right; awards that are themselves a share of the record are deliberately left out, so it cannot feed on itself

readBy.note: a crew member whose own standing in that trade falls short of a small fraction of the record, plus a little besides, is topped up to it - which is how a fresh recruit starts at a level worth having
while the crew are sharing what they know, a proportion of the record is granted in every trade at once
a twentieth of the record is handed to everyone aboard and everyone in the reserve, for trades the crew have already put real work into

globalVars.notes: There is one of these for every trade in the game, including ones the player can never take up. The topping-up compares against a character's lifetime standing in the trade rather than their current one, so it does not undo the cost of retraining. Nothing resets any of them, and they are what makes later recruits arrive far stronger than the first ones did.

globalVars.name: {actorID}_xp

params.name: actorID
params.note: one for each member of the player's crew at the moment a sea battle begins

globalVars.description: A note of how far along one crew member was in their trade just before a sea battle. It is taken for every hand aboard as the fleets close, and it is what lets the report afterwards say who learned what: each person's standing is measured against the note and the gain shown beside their portrait, with everyone who gained the same amount listed together.

setBy.note: taken for every hand in the player's fleet as the battle is entered, alongside the note of where the ship was left

readBy.note: subtracted from a crew member's standing when the after-battle report is drawn; anyone who gained nothing is left out of the list entirely

globalVars.notes: Only a person's standing in the trade they are practising is noted, so someone who changes trade during the battle is measured against a note taken for a different one and the report will overstate or understate them. The notes are never cleared, and one is left behind for every person who has ever been in the crew when a battle began. Nothing is noted for crew who are ashore in the reserve.

globalVars.name: {actorValueID}_bonus

params.name: actorValueID
params.note: any lasting, beneficial trait a person carries; the two hidden true-maximum figures for health and magic are deliberately excluded

globalVars.description: A standing bonus to one of a person's traits, granted to everyone the player commands. It is folded in whenever a character's standing bonuses are worked out again - on being recruited, on changing gear or trade, and whenever the crew are brought up to date - and is invisible in the breakdown of where a trait's value comes from. There is no built-in setter; it exists so a mod can make the player's whole company better at something at once.

setBy.note: nothing in the game or its content writes one; left alone the bonus is nothing and is skipped entirely

readBy.note: added to the named trait for each person the player commands; for the two capacity traits the same amount is also poured into the pool itself, so raising a person's ceiling does not leave them short

globalVars.notes: It reaches only people the player commands, and never ships - a fleet's vessels are left out. It does not apply to traits that count against a person, nor to the two hidden true-maximum figures behind health and magic, so those cannot be raised this way. The bonus is torn down and rebuilt on every refresh rather than accumulating, so changing it takes effect the next time that character is brought up to date. Filling the health and magic pools only makes up what the character is missing, so it will not overfill someone already whole.

globalVars.name: {factionID}_battleFleetsSpawned

params.name: factionID
params.note: any faction that puts fleets to sea; the game keeps one for each of the four nations

globalVars.description: A stamp recording when a nation last sent a warfleet out. What matters is not the tally itself but how recently it was touched: a nation that has just put out a squadron will not send another for the best part of a day, then does so at a modest rate, and only after several days does it fall back to sending them out as freely as its treasury allows. It is what keeps warfleets trickling onto the map rather than appearing all at once.

setBy.note: stamped afresh every time that nation puts a warfleet to sea, the count going up by one as a side effect

readBy.note: a nation short of warships asks how long it has been: nothing within a day, a chance in proportion to its wealth after that, and twice as good a chance once several days have gone by
a nation already at strength but below its limit only builds at all once several days have passed, and then at half the rate

globalVars.notes: The number itself is never read - only the moment it was last written - so a mod that wants to know how many warfleets a nation has raised can use it, but a mod that writes to it is really resetting the nation's cooldown. A nation that has never raised one counts as having waited forever, so the first squadron can appear immediately. Nothing clears it.

globalVars.name: {factionID}_merchantFleetsSpawned

params.name: factionID
params.note: any faction that puts fleets to sea; the game keeps one for each of the four nations

globalVars.description: A stamp recording when a nation last sent a trading convoy out. What matters is how recently it was touched rather than the tally itself: a nation that has just sent one out will not send another for the best part of a day, then sends them at a rate set by its wealth, and only after several days does it send them as freely as it can. It is what keeps merchant traffic appearing steadily instead of all at once.

setBy.note: stamped afresh every time that nation puts a trading convoy to sea, the count going up by one as a side effect

readBy.note: a nation with too few convoys at sea asks how long it has been: nothing within a day, a chance in proportion to its wealth after that, and twice as good a chance once several days have gone by
a nation already trading in strength but below its limit only sends more once several days have passed, and then at half the rate

globalVars.notes: The number itself is never read - only the moment it was last written - so writing to it is really resetting the nation's cooldown rather than telling it how many convoys it has sent. A nation that has never sent one counts as having waited forever, so its first convoy can appear immediately. Nothing clears it. Since sailing preys on this traffic, holding it back starves the sea of prizes.

globalVars.name: {levelDataID}_{pieceKey}

params.name: levelDataID
params.note: the kind of place being laid out, which is what makes the memory particular to that kind of wilderness or ruin

params.name: pieceKey
params.note: the name a layout gives to one of its must-have features, grouping the alternatives that can fill that slot

globalVars.description: Remembers which of the alternatives was used last time for one of a place's must-have features - the hidden chamber a jungle always contains, say. When that kind of place is laid out afresh the game rolls again until it comes up with something different, so a player exploring the same sort of wilderness twice does not walk into the same set-piece both times.

setBy.note: written with whatever was chosen, once the reroll has settled, each time a place of that kind is laid out

readBy.note: the choice is rerolled for as long as it matches what is remembered, so the same feature cannot appear two visits running

globalVars.notes: The avoidance only applies where a layout picks its features at random and has more than one alternative to choose between; a layout that works through its features in a fixed order writes the memory but never consults it. Only the immediately preceding choice is remembered, so with two alternatives the two simply take turns. Nothing clears it, and a mod that trims a slot down to a single alternative while the memory still holds that one leaves the game rerolling forever.

globalVars.name: {locationID}_dojo1

params.name: locationID
params.note: the port the fighting school stands in; seven ports have one

globalVars.description: Marks that the fighting school in one port has been beaten. It goes up as the player walks out of the training floor with no one left standing, and afterwards the master no longer offers the challenge - the player is congratulated instead, given the run of the place to train in, and their name as a fighter spreads. Beating all seven schools is an achievement in its own right.

setBy.note: raised on stepping off the training floor, but only once nothing hostile is still standing on it

readBy.note: the offer to fight is withdrawn once the school has been beaten, and the master's greeting turns to congratulation, a standing welcome to train, and a lift to the player's reputation as a fighter
having all seven raised at once earns the achievement for clearing every school

globalVars.notes: Only the seven schools the game ships with are counted towards the achievement, and their names are fixed, so a mod adding an eighth school cannot add it to that reckoning. Nothing lowers one, so a school stays beaten for good. The mark is raised on leaving the floor rather than on the last opponent falling, so a player who withdraws while enemies still stand gets nothing.

globalVars.name: {setPieceID}_added

params.name: setPieceID
params.note: any of the game's prefabricated chunks of map; one tally exists for each

globalVars.description: How many times one prefabricated chunk of map has been laid into a generated place over the course of the game. Its purpose is to let a layout wear a feature out: the guarded clearing that groves are built around keeps appearing until it has been used some thirty times, after which groves start offering their other centrepiece instead. All the tallies are wiped whenever the world's generated places are built afresh.

setBy.note: counted once for each chunk successfully fitted into a place, after the ground around it has been reshaped to suit
every tally in the game is zeroed when the world's generated places are thrown away and rebuilt

readBy.note: the guarded clearing is passed over once its tally has run past about thirty, leaving groves to fall back on their other centrepiece

globalVars.notes: A chunk that fails to fit is not counted, so the tally counts what is actually in the world rather than what was attempted. Nothing bounds it, and it survives ordinary play indefinitely; only the full rebuild of the generated world clears it. A mod that wants a feature to run out after so many uses can read its own tally the same way, but should expect the count to reach back over the whole save rather than the current expedition.

globalVars.name: {setPieceID}_added_temp

params.name: setPieceID
params.note: any of the game's prefabricated chunks of map; a tally appears for each one used

globalVars.description: How many times one prefabricated chunk of map has gone into the place currently being built. It rises alongside the lifetime tally as each chunk is fitted, and every one of these running tallies is wiped clean the moment the place is finished and the player is set down in it, so it only ever describes the layout being made. Nothing in the game consults it.

setBy.note: counted once for each chunk successfully fitted, in step with the lifetime tally
every one of these running tallies is zeroed as the place is finished, so the next place starts from nothing

globalVars.notes: It exists for a mod to limit how often a feature can appear within a single generated place, which the lifetime tally cannot express - but no part of the game uses it, so it is a hook rather than a working mechanism. The wipe finds these tallies by their names alone, so any name a mod invents ending the same way is cleared with them. Zeroed rather than removed, so once a chunk has been used the tally sticks around holding nothing.

globalVars.name: {zoneID}_merged

params.name: zoneID
params.note: the identifier of the add-on piece of map, not of the place it is folded into

globalVars.description: Marks that one add-on piece of map has already been folded into the place it belongs to. A mod can declare an extra piece to be grafted onto an existing place the first time the player walks in with its condition met - a new door in an old wall, say. The graft is permanent, and this is what stops it being applied a second time on every later visit.

setBy.note: raised as the graft is about to be carried out, once its condition has been found to hold

readBy.note: a graft already marked is passed over on entering the place, and the rest of the entry goes on as normal

globalVars.notes: It is named after the add-on piece rather than the place receiving it, so one place taking several grafts keeps a separate mark for each. Nothing lowers it: once a graft has gone in, it stays in for the life of the save even if the condition that let it in stops holding, and a mod cannot arrange for a graft to be applied twice by any means short of clearing the mark itself. A place with no add-on piece declared for it never touches any of these.

globalVars.name: class_{actorClassID}

params.name: actorClassID
params.note: the trade being unlocked; the game uses this naming for the trades taught by masters rather than the handful anyone starts able to take up

globalVars.description: Marks that the player has been taught a trade and may now put their people into it. Each advanced trade has a master somewhere in the world who will teach it for a fee, and until the lesson has been paid for and taken, that trade is greyed out on the character sheet with training listed among what it still needs. Once the mark is up, anyone in the crew who meets the trade's other demands can take it up.

setBy.note: raised as the lesson concludes, after the fee is taken, with a flourish announcing the new trade
the developers' shortcut that opens every trade at once raises all of them together

readBy.note: a trade whose mark is down cannot be taken up by anyone, whatever their other qualifications
a trade still to be learned lists training among what it needs
a master who has already taught the player does not offer the lesson again

globalVars.notes: Whether a trade is gated this way is decided by the trade itself rather than by the game: each trade names the condition it wants, and most of the taught ones happen to name a mark of this shape. A mod adding a trade is free to gate it on anything at all, or on nothing. Nothing lowers a mark, so a trade once learned stays available for the rest of the save.

globalVars.name: elitefleetsDefeated_{factionID}

params.name: factionID
params.note: the beaten fleet's own faction, not the player's

globalVars.description: A lifetime tally of how many of one faction's elite fleets the player has destroyed at sea. These are the picked squadrons a nation sends out rather than its ordinary warships, so the tally rises far more rarely than the broader ones. A sovereign's errand to hunt down a nation's finest is judged against it.

setBy.note: raised by one when a won sea battle finishes and the beaten fleet was a picked squadron; the same victory also raises the war-fleet and all-fleets tallies

readBy.note: shown as the progress figure on an errand to destroy a nation's elite fleet
the errand is judged complete by comparing the tally for the named nation against the figure recorded when it was handed out

globalVars.notes: The victory has to run through the sinking and cargo-reduction step to count; a battle that ends some other way leaves the tally alone. Nothing ever resets it, so an errand measures the difference between the tally now and the tally when it was taken. An elite squadron counts towards all three tallies at once, since it is a war fleet as well.

globalVars.name: fame_{fameType}

params.name: fameType
params.note: one of explore, trade, combat or piracy; the first three are the standings shown on the pause menu and the fourth is kept out of sight

globalVars.description: How widely the player is known for one kind of deed - charting the unknown, driving a hard bargain, winning fights, or robbing ships. Each rises with the deeds themselves and never falls below nothing, and between them they decide what work is offered: which jobs a port has on its board, which errand a sovereign sends, how boldly nations put their best squadrons to sea against the player, and even how townsfolk address them. Renown also lifts the crew's spirits as it grows.

setBy.note: the ordinary way renown moves, held at nothing as a floor; the same change stirs the crew and prompts the nations to reconsider what errand to offer
some conversations add to a standing directly rather than going through the usual path, so the crew are not stirred and no errand is reconsidered

readBy.note: a sovereign will not send for the player at all until one standing passes a threshold that climbs with rank, and whichever standing is highest decides what kind of errand they are sent on
which jobs appear on a port's board: an unknown explorer sees fewer of them, while cargo and monster work is held back until the player has made a name in the right field
a player known as a fighter draws a nation's picked squadron out sooner
three of the standings are drawn on the pause menu with their names given on hover; the fourth is kept hidden
a well-known trader earns less renown from the same profit, so the trade standing slows as it rises
reaching a thousand in all three of the open standings is an achievement, as is five thousand in any one
the three open standings are also available to written conditions, summed together or taken at their highest, which is how content asks whether the player is famous enough yet

globalVars.notes: The piracy standing is kept but never shown, and unlike the others it changes quietly, with no figure floating up and no sound. Renown never goes below nothing, so losses are absorbed once a standing is already at the floor. Because the errand a sovereign offers keys off whichever standing is highest, a player who is strong in one field will keep being sent on that kind of errand.

globalVars.description: How well one faction thinks of the player. It rises with service and falls with piracy and with sinking their ships, and it is bounded: never worse than a deep disgrace, and never better than a ceiling that only rises as the player climbs the ranks in that faction's own service. Standing decides a great deal - whether their ports will open the gate, whether their fleets hail the player or open fire, what their traders charge, and what repairs cost.

setBy.note: the one way standing moves: held between deep disgrace and a ceiling that grows with the player's rank, doubled for gains with the player's own faction once they are high enough in it, and every change prompts the nations to reconsider what errand to offer
the pirates' account is set so far beyond reach at the start that nothing can bring it back

readBy.note: a port belonging to a faction that despises the player will not let them in at all
a warfleet of a faction that despises the player attacks on sight when the player sails within reach
hailing a fleet of a faction that despises the player gets a threat from a warship or a refusal from a trader instead of a conversation
provisions are cheaper where the player is well thought of and dearer where they are not
a well-regarded captain is charged less to have their ships put right
standing with a named faction is available to written conditions, which is how conversations and content gate what they offer on it

globalVars.notes: Only factions that keep account are affected; a change aimed at one that does not is simply dropped, so nothing is stored for them. The ceiling is worked out afresh on every change from the player's current rank in their own faction, so being promoted lets standing rise further than before, while leaving that faction's service caps it back down at the next change. The floor is a deep disgrace rather than zero, so a faction can be well past the point of shooting on sight and still get worse.
